# Uniform local stability of the three-cap overlap inequality

This is an ordinary planar compactness theorem with an attained modulus.
It is not a quantitative mixed-fiber credit inequality. In particular, the
individual affine normalizations in the proof are used only to describe
one planar body; they are not applied independently to fibers of a mixed
source or asserted to preserve its lattice.

## 1. Statement

Let K be a planar convex body of area V, covered by three closed halfplanes
with areas A_i in K. Put

    E=sum_i A_i-V-(3/4)min_i A_i >=0.

The nonnegativity is the audited theorem in
`candidate e239a5fb0d0efe4d` and
`candidate 79c19cddb83423ea`.

For every tau>0 and eta>0 there exists epsilon(tau,eta)>0 such that

    min_i A_i>=tau V,             E<=epsilon(tau,eta) V

imply

    |A_i/V-4/9|<eta for every i.                         (1)

There is also a geometric version using an explicit normalization. Choose
any maximum-area inscribed triangle of K and map its vertices affinely to
(0,0),(1,0),(0,1), obtaining K*. The same epsilon may be chosen so that

    d_H(K*,T)<eta,       T=conv{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)}.       (2)

After normalizing each transformed cap normal to unit length and clipping
irrelevant full-cap offsets as specified below, the three cap parameters
are, up to permutation, within eta of the three canonical centroid caps
of T. No differentiability, strict convexity, rationality, or initial
inradius assumption is required.

## 2. A compact affine normalization with no selection gap

A maximum-area inscribed triangle exists: its area is a continuous
function of three points of compact K, and K has nonempty interior, so
the maximum is positive. An affine map taking one such triangle to T is
invertible. It scales all areas by one common determinant, preserving the
ratios A_i/V and E/V and the covering property.

For any x in the normalized body K*, let lambda_0,lambda_1,lambda_2 be
its barycentric coordinates with respect to T. Replacing vertex i of T
by x gives a triangle of area |lambda_i|/2. Maximality therefore gives
|lambda_i|<=1 for each i. Consequently

    T subset K* subset Q,
    Q={x: |lambda_i(x)|<=1 for i=0,1,2}.

The set Q is the fixed triangle with vertices (1,1),(1,-1),(-1,1), so it
is compact and lies in the ball of radius 2 about 0. Every inscribed
triangle in K* has area at most 1/2, and V*>=1/2.

Let C be the class of all convex bodies L with T subset L subset Q and
maximum inscribed-triangle area at most 1/2. This class is compact in
Hausdorff distance. For completeness, its support functions on the unit
circle are uniformly bounded and are 2-Lipschitz because all L lie in
the radius-two ball. Arzela--Ascoli yields a uniformly convergent
subsequence of any sequence of such support functions. Its limiting
closed convex set is the intersection of the limiting supporting
halfplanes. It contains T and lies in Q; uniform support convergence is
Hausdorff convergence for compact convex sets. Any triangle in the limit
can be approximated vertexwise by triangles in the sequence, so its area
is at most 1/2. Thus the limiting body is still in C.

Transform and normalize each halfplane to {x:u_i.x>=b_i}, |u_i|=1. A
positive-area cap has b_i<2 since L subset the radius-two ball. If b_i<-2,
replace b_i by -2. This preserves its trace on every such L because
u_i.x>=-2 throughout L. Thus positive-cap traces may be represented by
parameters in the compact set

    (S^1 x [-2,2])^3.

Only a full trace can have been changed by this clipping, and its trace,
area, and the covering property remain exactly the same.

## 3. All required limits

Consider L_j converging to L in C and cap parameters converging to
(u_i,b_i), with |u_i|=1. The indicators of L_j converge almost everywhere
to that of L: points in int(L) are eventually in L_j and points outside
L are eventually outside L_j, while the boundary of a full-dimensional
convex body has area zero. This can also be seen directly by contracting
L toward an interior point, using uniform support convergence. Likewise
the cap indicators converge off their limiting boundary lines, which have
area zero. All sets lie in a fixed ball. Dominated convergence therefore
gives convergence of V_j and every A_(i,j), hence of E_j and their
normalized ratios. The denominators remain at least 1/2.

Covering is closed under these limits. For x in L choose x_j in L_j with
x_j -> x. Each x_j lies in at least one of the three closed halfplanes.
Along a subsequence one fixed index contains x_j, so its limiting closed
inequality contains x. Thus the limiting caps cover L.

It follows that the class C_tau of normalized covered bodies and clipped
cap parameters satisfying A_i>=tau V for every i is compact. In particular,
no cap disappears in its limits. If tau>1 this class is simply empty.

## 4. Attained positive modulus and the equality limit

The audited equality theorem
`candidate 885e76d204f3f3f5` says that
E=0 and all A_i>0 force L to be a triangle with its three canonical
centroid vertex caps. Because L belongs to C and contains T, this triangle
must be T itself: its area is at most 1/2 by the maximum-triangle condition
and at least 1/2 by containment. Equal-area containment of full-dimensional
compact convex bodies gives equality of the bodies. The three limiting
caps consequently have areas 4V/9 and their parameters are the canonical
ones, up to permutation.

Explicitly these canonical parameters are

    ((1,0),1/3),
    ((0,1),1/3),
    ((-1,-1)/sqrt(2), -2/[3 sqrt(2)]).

Define D(L,H) as the maximum of the following continuous quantities:

* max_i |A_i/V-4/9|;
* d_H(L,T);
* the minimum, over the six permutations, of the maximum Euclidean
  parameter distance between the three (u_i,b_i) and those canonical
  parameters.

The subset of C_tau with D>=eta is compact. If it is nonempty, the
continuous nonnegative functional E/V attains a minimum m(tau,eta) on it.
This minimum is strictly positive: a zero value would have D=0 by the
equality classification, contradicting eta>0. Define

    epsilon(tau,eta)=m(tau,eta)/2

in this case, and define epsilon(tau,eta)=1 if that subset is empty.
These definitions prove a positive, attained modulus without any illicit
interchange of an infimum and a limit. If E/V<=epsilon, then D<eta,
which proves (1), (2), and the cap-parameter assertion simultaneously.

The argument works for every choice of maximum-area inscribed triangle:
each such normalization belongs to the same compact class C.

## 5. An explicit threshold-tightening surplus bound

There is one useful quantitative estimate independent of this modulus.
For a positive-circuit triple covering the whole plane, tighten its
thresholds to concurrence as in the overlap theorem. Let A_i'<=A_i be
the resulting cap areas and let delta_i=A_i-A_i'. Then

    E >= (1/4)sum_i delta_i.                             (3)

Indeed F(A)-F(A')>= (1-r)sum delta_i for r=3/4, while F(A')>=V.
More generally the rank-two theorem in dimension d gives
E_d>= (1-r_d)sum delta_i.

In particular, if min A_i>=tau V and E<=tau V/8 in the planar case,
then min A_i'>=tau V-4E>=tau V/2. Thus a small-surplus proper cover has
both small total annular mass lost by tightening and a positive-minimum
concurrent cover to which the same stability theorem applies.

Neither (3) nor the qualitative modulus proves that the sum of local
surpluses pays the mixed-fiber dispersion term. The actual-critical
example in `candidate c4ec563040ba09b3`
shows why those surpluses cannot simply be discarded. A bound in the
sub-OC regime still requires an additional proved global argument.

## 6. A proved deficit localization that retains the small-budget premise

Consider a finite mixed family of positive planar fibers of total area M,
partitioned into k ownership groups. Each group has three actual ambient
caps covering every fiber it owns; every selected global cap mass is at
most B. Repeated cap occurrences cause no problem. Let E_z be the local
surplus from Section 1 on its owned fiber, and set

    E_tot=sum_z E_z,
    W_tau=sum_{z: min_j A_j(z)<tau V_z} V_z.

Suppose the cap budget has a strict deficit

    k B <= (4/9-delta) M,                delta>0.         (4)

The ordinary three-cap union bound gives k B>=M/3, so necessarily
0<delta<=1/9. Choose any eta in (0,delta), and put
epsilon=epsilon(tau,eta) from Section 4. Then

    W_tau + E_tot/epsilon
      >= [(delta-eta)/(1/9-eta)] M.                    (5)

This inequality applies to actual caps and retains (4) explicitly.
For instance eta=delta/2 gives the coefficient
(delta/2)/(1/9-delta/2)>0.

To prove it, call a fiber good if min A_j>=tau V_z and E_z<=epsilon V_z.
On good fibers every A_j/V_z>=4/9-eta by stability; thus the average of
the three captured areas is at least (4/9-eta)V_z. On every other fiber
that average is at least V_z/3 by covering. The total area of nongood
fibers is at most W_tau+E_tot/epsilon. Summing these lower bounds, while
retaining that the sum of owned cap areas is at most 3k B, yields

    k B >= (4/9-eta)M
           -(1/9-eta)(W_tau+E_tot/epsilon).

Combining with (4) proves (5).

Thus a subthreshold cover cannot have both negligible total local surplus
and negligible mass on fibers with a small local cap. This is a proved
alternative, not a proof that either of those two quantities can be
eliminated at a mixed-integer extremizer. It does not replace the missing
arithmetic/deformation step.
